members.note: EDreamPanelHorizontalAlignment. On the control rather than in the style: where a thing sits is that thing's business, and two borders sharing a sheet hold different things.

A Slate border draws its content through a greyscale effect while disabled, and this opts out of it. Nothing here has such an effect to opt out of: a disabled look is a selectable's state colours, and a border carries no selectable.

The control takes UMG's FLinearColor and spends its ALPHA on the content node's RenderOpacity, which is the one channel that cascades here -- so fading a border fades everything in it, whatever each thing is drawn with. The colour half is deliberately not faked: a colour over a subtree would have to be written onto each visual inside, overwriting what the host authored with no way back.
In the style, because it is one quantity and a second copy on the control is how the two learn to disagree. GetPadding answers the RESOLVED number; SetPadding edits this instance's style.
FDreamUIFaceBrush rather than FSlateBrush -- a control face is a procedural rect, and the brush is its body texture. See the struct's own note.
FColor, and a TINT over the style's background colour -- which is what it is in Slate too.

On the PANEL spelling of a border, where it already scales what the panel reports (MeasureLayout multiplies the result and arranges the content in the rect it actually got -- UBorder's rule exactly). The control's face deliberately keeps an overlay instead: the border container pushes its own BrushColor onto the owning visual through FLinearColor::ToFColor(sRGB), so swapping containers would move every existing border's background through a gamma conversion. A project that needs the report scaled uses the panel, or wraps the control in one.

Mirroring is the PANEL's here, not each widget's: every panel that arranges through CommitChildRect reflects its children across its own width when the flow is right-to-left, so a border's content mirrors with everything else rather than by its own flag. UMG needs a per-widget opt-out because Slate mirrors by default; here a subtree that must not mirror states its flow direction.

A multicast carrying UDreamPointerEventData, not UMG's FEventReply-returning single binding: nothing in this event system asks a handler per call whether the event carries on. That answer is one property for all four -- bConsumeMouseEvents, which is UUIEventTrigger::AllowEventBubbleUp inverted. Gated on bReportMouseEvents, off by default, because a listening border is a consuming border.

Fed by the DRAG seam: this event system reports a moving pointer to the element it pressed on, which is the only motion a border can honestly claim. A hover that never pressed is OnPointerEnter/Exit, which UMG spells elsewhere.

Read off the click's own ClickCount being even, which is the event system's own rule (its DoubleClickTime, and a click on another widget starting the count over) rather than a second rule that could disagree with it.
Same half-and-half as the property above.
Pushed straight onto the content slot.
Takes FDreamUIFaceBrush; see Background above for why that is not FSlateBrush.

USlateBrushAsset wraps an FSlateBrush, which a procedural rect face cannot draw. The two things this framework's face brush takes -- a texture and an atlas sprite -- are what SetBrush and SetBrushFromTexture take.
Replaces the image and leaves the nine-slice, the scale mode and the tint where they were.

A procedural rect has no material of its own to set. Its material is GetMaterialToCreateGeometry -- the shared one the canvas batches every rect with -- and there is no per-instance override anywhere on UDreamVisual (the CustomUIMaterial the comments mention is a leftover name from the upstream library; nothing in this plugin declares it). The two visuals that do carry a material, UDreamText and UDreamImage, are what a material-drawn face is: put one inside the border. SetBrushFromSprite is here instead, which is the thing this face CAN take and Slate cannot.
Waits on nothing: see bShowEffectWhenDisabled.

The only dynamic instance a rect ever sees is the DRAW CALL's, handed to it after the fact (OnMaterialInstanceDynamicCreated) and shared with every other widget batched into the same call. Returning it would let a caller recolour a whole screen by setting one border's parameter.
See DesiredSizeScale above.
UBorder has no style struct at all; this is the family's spelling of replacing a look at runtime.
